title: Come and see
hook: a song of praise that stops to say: don't take my word for it
carry: ehipassiko: the dhamma asks to be tested
tomorrow: what does Ông chant before he drives home in the dark?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the teaching of the Buddhas: stop the harm, take up the good, clear your own mind. The heart in Pali. Today, a verse that praises that teaching, with a twist.
screen: `THE HEART IN PALI.` → `NOW, A VERSE OF PRAISE.`

segments.voice: A restaurant with a sign in the window that says don't trust our reviews, come taste it, would get your attention. Praise usually asks to be believed: five stars, best in town, life-changing. Buddhist chanting books have a verse of praise for the dhamma, the teaching, and right in the middle of it sits an odd word: ehipassiko. Come and see. A song meant to honor something stops halfway to say, in effect, don't take my word for it. So why would anyone put that in a hymn?
screen: `DON'T TRUST OUR REVIEWS.` → `A VERSE OF PRAISE FOR THE DHAMMA.` → `WHY SAY COME AND SEE?`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, as it's chanted. Svakkhato bhagavata dhammo: well taught by the Blessed One is the dhamma. Then its qualities, one after another. Sanditthiko: visible here and now, in this life. Akaliko: not a matter of time, nothing you wait ages for. Ehipassiko: from ehi, come, and passa, see. Of the come-and-see kind. Opanayiko: leading onward. And the last line: paccattam veditabbo vinnuhi, to be known by the wise, each for themselves. So the puzzle has its answer. The praise is the invitation. What the verse honors about the teaching is that it can be checked, here and now, in a life. But look at that last word, vinnuhi: by the wise. Come and see doesn't mean anything goes. In the talk to the Kalamas, villagers tired of rival teachers, the Buddha lists things not to lean on alone: reports, tradition, scripture, even clever reasoning. The test he offers is what a teaching does when it's lived. Does it lead to harm and suffering, or to welfare and happiness? And would the wise blame it or praise it? So come and see, and look closely, in good company.
screen: `A VERSE THAT PRAISES THE DHAMMA.` · `EHIPASSIKO: COME AND SEE.` · `KNOWN BY THE WISE, EACH FOR THEMSELVES.` · `NOT ANYTHING GOES: WHAT DOES IT DO?` · then, large: `COME AND SEE.`

segments.voice: Chant the dhamma verse once, slowly, from the screen. Then write ehipassiko on any scrap of paper, and under it one teaching from these weeks you'd like to test, maybe hatred never ends by hatred. For the rest of the sit, hold it up against one real memory of your own, and just look at what happened.
screen: `SVAKKHATO BHAGAVATA DHAMMO,` · `SANDITTHIKO AKALIKO EHIPASSIKO,` · `OPANAYIKO PACCATTAM VEDITABBO VINNUHI.`

segments.voice: Come and see: ehipassiko, from ehi, come, and passa, see. A teaching praised because you can check it yourself.
Hold on to this: ehipassiko, the dhamma asks to be tested. Come and see, then look closely, in good company. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Theravada temples the verse on the qualities of the dhamma is chanted in Pali after the verse on the Buddha's qualities and before the one on the sangha, often in morning and evening chanting.

match.prompt: the dhamma's qualities — tap the pairs.
pairs: known by the wise, each for themselves

myth: the Buddha said: believe nothing unless it agrees with your own reason
a popular paraphrase, not the text. the Kalama talk even lists clever reasoning among things not to lean on alone.
ehipassiko is built from ehi, come, and passa, see
come and see: a teaching of the kind you can check for yourself.
come and see means each person decides what's true, no help needed
the verse says known by the wise, each for themselves, and the Kalama test asks what the wise would blame or praise.

fork.setup: a new app promises your anxiety gone in seven days, guaranteed, and the reviews glow. by the dhamma verse's own test, what's your move?
options: trust it: that many good reviews can't be wrong.
try it, watch honestly what it does in your life, and ask someone wise.
skip it: anything that promises results must be a scam.
fork.reveal: come and see: check a teaching by what it does when lived, here and now, and bring the wise into it. not blind trust, not blanket rejection.

original.note: Pali, in Devanagari letters: ehi, come, and passa, see; 'of the come-and-see kind'.

trapdoor: what you thought: a friendly slogan, come and see, like a shop sign.
what it means: one quality in a chanted verse of praise: the dhamma is visible here and now, timeless, come-and-see, leading onward, known by the wise each for themselves.
what a scholar hears: the praise is the testability itself; and the Kalama talk keeps it from meaning 'anything goes': lived results, and what the wise blame or praise.
guess: an invitation to check the teaching for yourself
a welcome to visitors walking into a temple hall
a promise that awakening comes quickly to all

chat.says: Ava asked if i actually believe my mural line or just paint it for ông. awkward. what do i say?
options: Honest: you're testing it. The teaching itself says come and see, know it yourself.
Say yes. Doubting a line from your own family's tradition is disrespectful.
Say it doesn't matter. Buddhists believe whatever feels right to each person.
chat.meaning: The dhamma is praised as ehipassiko, come and see, known by the wise each for themselves. Testing it is the invitation.

tie.story: Tired of rival teachers, the Kalamas asked the Buddha whom to trust; he said to judge a teaching by what it does when lived, and what the wise praise.
tie.friend: Mai can tell Ava she's testing the line, which is exactly what the dhamma invites.
tie.you: What teaching are you testing right now?

ehipassiko.meaning: of the come-and-see kind: open to checking

Kalamas.meaning: villagers who asked the Buddha how to judge rival teachers

akaliko.meaning: not a matter of time; nothing to wait ages for

sources.ref: SN 11.3 (Dhajagga Sutta): the qualities of the dhamma, svakkhato bhagavata dhammo … paccattam veditabbo vinnuhi
AN 3.65 (Kalama Sutta): not by reports, tradition, scripture or reasoning alone; what leads to harm or welfare, blamed or praised by the wise

notes: The dhamma formula (svakkhato … vinnuhi) is the standard Pali recollection found in SN 11.3, DN 16 (the mirror of the dhamma) and elsewhere; meanings paraphrased after the PTS dictionary. Confirm 'akaliko: not a matter of time' and 'opanayiko: leading onward'.

ehipassiko = ehi + passa: the compound's parts are standard in Pali grammar and the PTS dictionary ('inviting to come and see'). Confirm it is fair to present as the word's parts, since the claims rule limits etymology.

Kalama Sutta (AN 3.65) paraphrased: the list (reports, tradition, scripture, reasoning) is shortened from the sutta's ten; the test (harm or welfare; blamed or praised by the wise) follows the text. Year one (day 66) introduced the Kalamas; this day uses only the test, briefly.
Myth item 1 names the popular quote ('believe nothing … unless it agrees with your own reason') as a paraphrase, not the sutta's words. Confirm the Keeper is comfortable with that framing.
